name: Throughput vs Latency
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Fast Lane or Wide Lane? Untangling Throughput and Latency
lesson.summary: Throughput and latency are frequently confused but measure two different things: throughput is how many transactions a network can process per unit of time, while latency is how long any single transaction takes to be confirmed, and a blockchain can be strong on one while weak on the other.
lesson.body:
Transaction throughput, covered a few chapters back, measures a network's aggregate capacity, how many transactions it can process per second, on average, across the whole system. Latency, which depends heavily on network latency, the delay for information to travel between nodes, measures something different: how long it takes for one particular transaction, the one you just submitted, to go from broadcast to confirmed. A useful analogy is a highway. Throughput is how many cars per hour pass a given point on the road, its capacity. Latency is how long it takes any single car to complete its own trip. A highway can move a huge volume of cars per hour while any individual driver still sits in it for an hour, and a nearly empty road can offer a fast trip for one driver while carrying very little traffic overall. The two numbers are related but not the same, and a blockchain can be strong on one while weak on the other.

The divergence shows up clearly across real designs. Bitcoin batches transactions into blocks roughly every ten minutes, and because a single confirmation is not always considered final enough for high value transfers, users are often advised to wait for several additional blocks before treating a payment as settled, sometimes pushing effective latency for a cautious user well past thirty minutes. That long latency exists even though Bitcoin's aggregate throughput, roughly seven transactions per second, is a separate, independently limited number describing total capacity, not how long any one person waits.

Conversely, a network built for very short block times can offer low latency, confirmation in well under a second in some proof of stake or delegated proof of stake designs, without necessarily offering high sustained throughput, if each of those fast blocks can only hold a small number of transactions. A chain optimized purely to minimize the time until a block appears is not automatically optimized to maximize the number of transactions that block can carry.

This distinction matters directly for evaluating real world claims. A project advertising itself as the fastest blockchain is very often citing a latency figure, block time or confirmation speed, without saying anything about sustained throughput under real load, and the two claims are not interchangeable. A coffee shop accepting a blockchain payment cares mostly about latency, how long the customer stands at the counter waiting for confirmation. An exchange settling thousands of trades across many users at once cares mostly about throughput, whether the system can keep up with aggregate volume without a growing backlog.

Keeping these two numbers separate is one of the more useful analytical habits this book tries to build, because marketing materials for new blockchain projects routinely quote whichever of the two numbers looks more impressive, and a reader who does not distinguish them has no way to tell whether a genuinely meaningful improvement is being described or just one metric optimized at the expense of the other.
